meta.title: The Respiratory System in 3D
meta.one_body: This model shows one real adult body. Real people vary: sizes, angles, and shapes differ from person to person.
meta.left_right: Left and right always mean the person's own left and right. In the front view, the person's right side is on your left.
meta.lobe_colors: Lung lobes are tinted different colors only so you can tell them apart. Real lungs are all one pinkish color.
meta.vessel_colors: Blood vessels use the textbook code: red for oxygen-rich blood, blue for oxygen-poor blood.
meta.breathing_label: Simplified animation. The model comes from a still body, so real breathing motion is not in the data.
meta.illustration_label: Illustration, not to scale. Bronchioles and alveoli are too small to come from the body data.

missing: Cuneiform cartilages and the soft covering of the vocal folds are not in the source data.
The superior and middle nasal conchae are part of the ethmoid bone mesh, not separate pieces.
Bronchioles and alveoli are too small for the body data; they are shown as an illustration.

Some soft parts (the lung lobes, throat, nose lining, larger bronchi, and diaphragm) appear to have been rebuilt by the Z-Anatomy team to fit this body. They follow the real body's layout, but their surfaces were not traced straight from scan data.
The bronchi are shown as smooth tubes; real bronchi have cartilage plates in their walls.

landmarks.label: Cardiac notch
landmarks.source: Label anchor point from Z-Anatomy ('Cardiac notch of left lung'), moved onto the nearest lobe surface (0.6 mm).

landmarks.label: Lingula
landmarks.source: Label anchor point from Z-Anatomy ('Lingula of left lung'), moved onto the nearest lobe surface (0.2 mm).

nasal_cavity.function: Air comes in through your nostrils into the nasal cavity. Its lining cleans the air, warms it, and adds moisture.
facts: A wall called the nasal septum splits the nasal cavity into a left side and a right side.
The lining makes sticky mucus that traps dirt. Tiny hairs called cilia sweep the mucus toward your throat, where you swallow it.
Model note: this shows the soft lining of the nasal cavity. The air space is inside it.

inferior_nasal_conchae.function: Curled shelves of bone on the side walls of the nose. They make the air swirl so more of it touches the lining, where it gets cleaned and warmed.
facts: Each side of the nose has three conchae: superior (top), middle, and inferior (bottom).
The inferior conchae are their own separate bones.
When you breathe out, the conchae catch water, which keeps the inside of your nose from drying out.

ethmoid_bone.common: Ethmoid bone (with the superior and middle conchae)
ethmoid_bone.function: A light, thin skull bone between the eyes. Parts of it form the upper walls of the nasal cavity, including the superior and middle conchae.
facts: The superior and middle conchae are parts of the ethmoid bone.
The back part of the nasal septum is made partly by the ethmoid bone.
Model note: the source data does not split the superior and middle conchae from the rest of this bone, so they are shown together.
ethmoid_bone.short: Ethmoid bone (with the superior and middle conchae)

nasopharynx.function: The top part of the throat, behind the nose. Only air passes through it.
facts: The pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) sits at the top of the nasopharynx.
Tubes from your middle ears, called Eustachian tubes, open into it.
When you swallow, the soft palate and uvula swing up to close it off, so food does not go up into your nose.

oropharynx.function: The middle part of the throat, behind the mouth. Both air and food pass through it.
facts: The palatine tonsils and the lingual tonsil are found here.
Its lining is made of layers of flat cells that stand up to rubbing from food.
The whole pharynx is a tube of muscle lined with a mucous membrane.

laryngopharynx.function: The lowest part of the throat. Air and food both pass through it until their paths split.
facts: In front, it opens into the larynx, which leads to the lungs.
In back, it opens into the esophagus, which leads to the stomach.
Mucus swept up from the airways reaches the laryngopharynx and is swallowed.

epiglottis.function: A flap of bendy cartilage at the top of the larynx. When you swallow, it swings down and covers the opening to the trachea, so food goes into the esophagus instead.
facts: It is made of elastic cartilage, so it can bend and spring back.
When it is closed, it rests on the glottis (the vocal folds and the space between them).
If something does slip into the airway, nerves at the carina set off a strong cough to push it out.

thyroid_cartilage.function: The largest cartilage of the larynx. It forms the front of the larynx and protects the vocal folds behind it.
facts: The bump at its front is called the laryngeal prominence, or Adam's apple.
When you swallow, the larynx moves up. You can feel this by touching your throat.

cricoid_cartilage.function: A ring of cartilage at the bottom of the larynx. The trachea starts just below it.
facts: The ring is wide at the back and thinner at the front.
The larynx connects the pharynx above to the trachea below.

arytenoid_cartilages.function: A pair of small cartilages at the back of the larynx. The back ends of the vocal folds attach to them.
facts: They are one of three pairs of small cartilages in the larynx. The others are the corniculate and cuneiform cartilages.
There is one on the person's right and one on the person's left.

corniculate_cartilages.function: A pair of tiny cartilages that sit on top of the arytenoid cartilages.
facts: They are one of three pairs of small cartilages in the larynx.
Model note: the third pair, the cuneiform cartilages, is not in the source data, so it is not shown.

vocal_folds.function: Two bands of tissue that stretch across the larynx. When air from the lungs passes between them, they vibrate and make the sound of your voice.
facts: The glottis is made of the vocal folds and the space between them.
Males usually have larger vocal folds, which gives a deeper voice.

Model note: these meshes come from BodyParts3D (the vocal ligament and vocalis muscle inside each fold). They were placed using the larynx cartilages they attach to. The soft outer covering is not in the source data.

trachea.function: A tube that carries air from the larynx down into the chest. At the bottom it splits into the right and left main bronchi.
facts: 16 to 20 C-shaped rings of cartilage keep it open. In this model you can see the rings as raised bands (17 counted).
The open back of each C is closed by a muscle called the trachealis. The esophagus lies right behind it.
Its lining makes mucus that traps dirt and germs. Cilia beat the mucus up toward the throat.
In this model the trachea is 11.0 cm long.

right_main_bronchus.function: Carries air from the trachea into the right lung.
facts: It is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left main bronchus.
Because of this, objects that are breathed in by accident usually end up in the right lung.
The trachea splits into the two main bronchi at a ridge called the carina.

left_main_bronchus.function: Carries air from the trachea into the left lung.
facts: It is longer and narrower than the right main bronchus, and it runs more sideways.
On its way to the left lung it passes under the arch of the aorta and in front of the esophagus.
In this model it is 4.8 cm long, measured from the carina.

intermediate_bronchus.function: The part of the right airway after the upper lobe branch. It carries air on to the middle and lower lobes.
facts: The right main bronchus splits into the right upper lobe bronchus and the intermediate bronchus.
The intermediate bronchus then splits into the middle lobe and lower lobe bronchi.

right_upper_lobar_bronchus.function: A lobar (secondary) bronchus. It carries air into the right upper lobe.
facts: Each lobe has its own lobar bronchus: 3 on the right and 2 on the left.
The walls of the bronchi are held open by plates of cartilage.

seg_right_upper_b1.function: A segmental (tertiary) bronchus. It carries air into one bronchopulmonary segment, a section of a lung lobe.
facts: Each segment gets air from its own segmental bronchus and blood from its own artery.
Doctors can sometimes remove one diseased segment without harming the segments next to it.
The right lung has 10 segments. The left lung has 8 to 10, depending on how they are counted.
Model note: the model shows this bronchus and its first few branches.

right_upper_lobe.function: The top lobe of the right lung. Like every lobe, it ends in tiny air sacs called alveoli, where oxygen passes into the blood.
facts: The right lung has three lobes. Deep grooves called fissures separate them.
The horizontal fissure separates this lobe from the middle lobe.
Its top, the apex, rises into the base of the neck. In this model the apex is about 2.6 cm above the inner part of the clavicle.

right_middle_lobe.function: The middle lobe of the right lung. Only the right lung has a middle lobe.
facts: It sits between the horizontal fissure (above) and the oblique fissure (below).
The right lung is shorter and wider than the left lung.

right_lower_lobe.function: The bottom lobe of the right lung. Its base rests on the dome of the diaphragm.
facts: The oblique fissure separates it from the upper and middle lobes.
The right dome of the diaphragm sits higher than the left because the liver is below it. So the right lung is a bit shorter.

left_upper_lobe.function: The top lobe of the left lung. It includes the cardiac notch and the lingula.
facts: The cardiac notch is a dent in the front edge of the left lung that makes room for the heart.
The lingula is the lowest front part of this lobe, just below the cardiac notch. It is made of two bronchopulmonary segments.
The left lung has only two lobes and takes up less space than the right lung.

left_lower_lobe.function: The bottom lobe of the left lung. Its base rests on the left dome of the diaphragm.
facts: The oblique fissure separates it from the left upper lobe.
The left lung has only one fissure, so it has two lobes.

diaphragm.function: The main muscle for breathing. When it contracts, it pulls down and flattens. That makes the chest bigger, so air rushes into the lungs.
facts: It is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle and tendon under the lungs.
Breathing out at rest takes no muscle effort: the diaphragm relaxes and the stretchy lungs spring back.
The right side sits higher than the left because the liver is under it. In this model the right dome is 1.9 cm higher.
It is controlled by the phrenic nerves, which come from the neck (spinal nerves C3 to C5).

rib_right_1.function: A curved bone of the rib cage. The rib cage protects the lungs and heart and moves when you breathe.
facts: Ribs 1 to 7 are true ribs: their cartilage attaches straight to the sternum.
There are 24 ribs (12 pairs). Together with the sternum they protect the heart and lungs.
Muscles between the ribs (the external intercostals) lift the rib cage when you breathe in.
The first rib is hidden behind the clavicle, so the second rib is the highest one you can feel.
At the back it joins the T1 thoracic vertebra.

sternum.function: The flat bone in the middle of the chest. The ribs and clavicles connect to it.
facts: It has three parts: the manubrium (top), the body (middle), and the xiphoid process (bottom tip).
The sternal angle is where the manubrium meets the body. The second rib attaches there.
The trachea splits into the two main bronchi at about the level of the sternal angle.
The xiphoid process starts as cartilage and turns into bone in middle age.

clavicle_right.function: The collarbone. It connects the shoulder to the sternum.
facts: Its inner end joins the sternum at the sternoclavicular joint.
The first rib is hidden behind it.
The top of each lung rises above the inner part of the clavicle. In this model it is about 2.6 to 2.7 cm higher.

heart.function: Pumps blood. The right side sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen. The left side sends oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body.
facts: It sits between the lungs, with its tip (apex) pointing to the person's left.
It is about the size of a fist.
It has four chambers: two atria that receive blood and two ventricles that pump it out.
Model note: the four chambers are joined into one piece here.

aorta.function: The main artery of the body. It carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle out to the body.
facts: The left main bronchus passes under the arch of the aorta.
Model note: the source shows the aorta as a simple smooth tube. The branches to the head and arms are left out here.

pulmonary_trunk.function: A large artery that carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs.
facts: It splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries.
Pulmonary arteries are among the only arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood.
Color note: it is blue here only because textbooks use blue for oxygen-poor blood. Real arteries are not blue.

right_pulmonary_artery.function: Carries oxygen-poor blood into the right lung, where it picks up oxygen in the tiny air sacs.
facts: Its branches follow the branches of the bronchi.
Each bronchopulmonary segment gets its own artery branch.
Color note: blue is a textbook code for oxygen-poor blood, not the real color.

right_pulmonary_veins.function: Carry oxygen-rich blood from the right lung back to the heart's left atrium.
facts: They leave the lung at the hilum, the spot where the airways and blood vessels enter and exit.
Pulmonary veins are the only veins (after birth) that carry oxygen-rich blood.
Color note: red is a textbook code for oxygen-rich blood.

left_pulmonary_artery.function: Carries oxygen-poor blood into the left lung, where it picks up oxygen in the tiny air sacs.
facts: Its branches follow the branches of the bronchi.
Each bronchopulmonary segment gets its own artery branch.
Color note: blue is a textbook code for oxygen-poor blood, not the real color.

left_pulmonary_veins.function: Carry oxygen-rich blood from the left lung back to the heart's left atrium.
facts: They leave the lung at the hilum, the spot where the airways and blood vessels enter and exit.
Pulmonary veins are the only veins (after birth) that carry oxygen-rich blood.
Color note: red is a textbook code for oxygen-rich blood.

esophagus.function: The food tube. It carries food and drink from the pharynx down to the stomach. It is part of the digestive system, not the airway.
facts: It lies right behind the trachea.
It is about 25 cm (10 in) long and passes through an opening in the diaphragm.
Waves of muscle squeezing, called peristalsis, push food down.
When you are not swallowing, it stays flat and closed.

walkthrough.title: 1. Nose
walkthrough.text: Air enters through the nostrils into the nasal cavity. The conchae make the air swirl. Mucus traps dirt, and the lining warms the air.

walkthrough.title: 2. Pharynx (throat)
walkthrough.text: Air moves down through the pharynx: the nasopharynx, the oropharynx, then the laryngopharynx. Food uses the lower two parts too.

walkthrough.title: 3. Larynx (voice box)
walkthrough.text: Air passes the epiglottis and goes between the vocal folds. When you swallow, the epiglottis covers this opening so food goes to the esophagus.

walkthrough.title: 4. Trachea (windpipe)
walkthrough.text: The trachea is a tube held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. Its lining traps dust, and cilia sweep it back up to the throat.

walkthrough.title: 5. Bronchi
walkthrough.text: At the carina the trachea splits into the right and left main bronchi. They split into lobar bronchi (one per lobe), then segmental bronchi.

walkthrough.title: 6. Bronchioles
walkthrough.text: The bronchi keep branching, 20 or more times. The small tubes, about 1 mm wide, are called bronchioles. They have muscle in their walls but no cartilage.

walkthrough.title: 7. Alveoli
walkthrough.text: Bronchioles end in clusters of tiny air sacs called alveoli, each about 0.2 mm across. Oxygen moves through their very thin walls into the blood, and carbon dioxide moves out.

bronchioles.caption: A bronchiole branches into smaller and smaller tubes. The last ones lead to alveoli.

alveoli.caption: Each alveolus is wrapped in tiny blood vessels (capillaries). The wall between air and blood is about 0.5 micrometers thick.
